deep.reconstruction:
Context: notebook entry by Hilbert, c. 1888-89. It refers to his own review in the Jahrbuch ueber die Fortschritte der Mathematik (F. d. M.), Bd. 20, S. 102. That review is presumably of L. Maurer's 1888 Munich paper on the invariance groups of forms ('Ueber allgemeinere Invariantensysteme'); this identification is mine.

(0) Maurer's theorem as Hilbert uses it. Let F(x_1..x_N) be a form. Let G_F = {A in GL_N : F(Ax) = F(x)} be the group of linear substitutions leaving F invariant. Its continuous part (the identity component, in modern terms) admits a rational parametrization: there are rational functions A(t_1..t_r) of free parameters whose values sweep out the group. Modern reading: the identity component G_F^0 is unirational, in fact rational.

(1) Claimed generalization. Let X be an algebraic variety ('Gebilde') in P^{n} with coordinates x, of any dimension. Then all linear (projective) substitutions A with A(X) = X can be written with substitution coefficients that are rational functions of parameters.

(2) Proof sketch on the page.
- Choose forms f_1..f_k of one and the same degree d whose common zeros define X. Hilbert inserted 'gleicher Ordnung' as a correction.
- Introduce indeterminate parameters lambda_1..lambda_k and form F(x, lambda) = sum_i lambda_i f_i(x). Treat the lambda as additional variables.
- Implicit step (mine): choose d so that the f_i span the whole degree-d part of the ideal of X. Then any A with A(X) = X satisfies f_i(Ax) = sum_j c_ij(A) f_j(x).
- Hence F(Ax, lambda) = sum_j (C^T lambda)_j f_j(x). So the block substitution (x, lambda) -> (Ax, C^{-T} lambda) leaves F invariant.
- Conversely, a block substitution leaving F invariant maps X to itself.
- So Stab(X) is the image of a subgroup of the invariance group of F. Maurer's theorem applied to F gives a rational parametrization; projecting to the x-block gives one for Stab(X).

(3) Corollary. A one-dimensional algebraic curve admitting a continuous group of (linear) transformations into itself is necessarily rational.
- Implicit argument (mine): by (1) the group is rationally parametrized. The orbit map t -> A(t)p from the parameter space onto the curve is rational and dominant, so the curve is unirational. By Lueroth's theorem it is then rational.

(4) Converse sketch (continued on the next page). Maurer's theorem should follow from (3). Single out those transformations that keep certain points fixed or send them to given points, so that a one-parameter subgroup maps some one-dimensional subvariety into itself. By (3) that subvariety is rational, which yields a rational parametrization of the one-parameter subgroup. Repeat with other one-parameter subgroups until the general element is a product of such one-parameter pieces. The product map then gives the rational parametrization.

Next page adds: for two forms, apply the theorem to their product.
errors: 'Alle linearen Substitutionen' is too strong. Maurer-type results only give a rational parametrization of the continuous part (identity component). Finite or discrete components, e.g. finite projective automorphism groups of a variety, are not covered by one rational family.
The reduction in (2) tacitly needs the f_i to span the full degree-d piece of the (saturated) ideal of X. Otherwise f_i(Ax) need not be a linear combination of the f_j.

The reduction in (2) also tacitly needs the invariance group of F in all variables (x, lambda) to be restricted to block substitutions; Hilbert does not address this. A further unstated point: the projection of a rationally parametrized group onto the x-block is again rationally parametrized (true, but unstated).

Corollary (3) is correct only for linear (projective) transformations of an embedded curve. For birational transformations it fails: elliptic curves have a continuous group of translations. 'continuirlichen Transformationen' must be read as linear substitutions as in the preceding sentence.

The converse (4) is only a sketch. It is not shown that the group is generated by finitely many one-parameter subgroups each of which preserves a curve, nor that the product parametrization covers the whole identity component. It yields unirationality, which is what 'rationale Funktionen der Parameter' asserts.
Maurer's original arguments were later regarded as incomplete in places. The rigorous modern version (rationality of connected linear algebraic groups) is due to Chevalley/Borel in the 1950s.

results.what: Hilbert's citation of Maurer's theorem: the continuous group of linear substitutions leaving a form invariant is rationally parametrizable
results.modern_name: Rationality/unirationality of connected linear algebraic groups (stabilizers of forms)
results.usually_credited_to: L. Maurer (1888, 1894); rigorous modern form Chevalley (1951-54), Borel (via the Bruhat big cell)

results.what: Extension from forms to the projective automorphism group of an arbitrary algebraic variety, by encoding the defining forms in one form F = sum lambda_i f_i with auxiliary variables
results.modern_name: Stab(X) of a projective variety is a linear algebraic group (stabilizer of a subspace of the degree-d part of the ideal), hence its identity component is rational
results.usually_credited_to: Standard in the 20th-century theory of algebraic groups (Chevalley); the trick of linearizing via the degree-d part of the ideal is folklore

results.what: A curve with a continuous group of linear self-transformations is rational
results.modern_name: Curves with infinite group of projective automorphisms have genus 0 (Lueroth + orbit map; cf. Schwarz/Hurwitz finiteness of automorphisms for genus >= 2)
results.usually_credited_to: Schwarz (1879), Klein, Hurwitz (1893) for finiteness in genus >= 2; Lueroth (1876)

results.what: Converse: Maurer's theorem deduced from the curve statement by decomposing into one-parameter subgroups preserving curves
results.modern_name: Unirationality of connected groups generated by rational one-parameter subgroups (product map)

deep.surprise_reason: Hilbert's review of Maurer's work is known, as is his involvement in invariant theory around 1888. A private sketch extending Maurer's rationality theorem to automorphism groups of arbitrary varieties, with an equivalence to the rationality of curves admitting continuous linear groups, is a notable unpublished detail. It is also an early 'algebraic group' viewpoint. But the ideas are sketchy, partly overstated, and were common currency in the Lie/Klein circle, so this is not a major priority claim.

Cayley transform: a rational one-parameter family of linear substitutions leaving the form x^2+y^2-z^2 invariant (Maurer-type rational parametrization of a rotation subgroup).
